#Question 2: rep(c("A","B"), each = 2) and rep(c("A","B"), times = 2) both produce a vector of length 4, but with different element orders.

#Answer: The each argument repeats items one by one (like "A" "A" "B" "B"). The times argument repeats the whole list all at once (like "A" "B" "A" "B").

#Question 3: Compare seq(1, 20, by = 2) with seq(1, 20, length.out = 5). What does each argument (by vs length.out) control, and when would you use one over the other in a real analysis?

#Answer:The by argument tells R exactly how much to skip or count by between each number (like counting by 2s). The length.out argument tells R exactly how many numbers you want in total, and R figures out how to space them out for you. Basically, use by when you know the exact gap you want, and use length.out when you just need a specific amount of numbers.

#Question 5: Negative indexing (grades[-1]) removes an element, while logical indexing (grades[grades >= 85]) filters by a condition.
#Describe a real situation where you would need negative indexing, and a different situation where logical indexing would be the better tool.

#Answer: Negative indexing removes an item by its position number, which is useful when you want to delete data you don't need, like an extra ID column. On the other hand, logical indexing uses a True or False rule to filter data, which you use when you only want to keep the data that exactly matches what you are looking for.

#Question 6: What happens if you run grades[10] (an index that doesn’t exist)? Run it, observe the result, and explain why R responds this way instead of throwing an error.

#Answer: Running grades[10] gives you NA (Not Available) instead of an error. R does this to safely show that there is no data at that specific spot, which allows your code to keep running smoothly without crashing just because a value is missing.

```{r}

```

#Question 8: In the vectors-recycling chunk, z has 6 elements and short has only 2. R still produced an answer instead of an error.
#Explain, in your own words, what R’s “recycling rule” did to short to make the addition work.

#Answer: R's "recycling rule" just repeats the shorter list over and over until it is as long as the longer one, so it can add them together perfectly.

#Question 9: Then try adding z to c(1, 0, 1, 1) (length 4). Compare the warning (or lack of one) in each case, and explain what condition determines whether R recycles silently versus with a warning.

#Answer: If the length of the longer list is an exact multiple of the shorter one (like 6 and 3), it works perfectly. If it is not (like 6 and 4), R gives a warning because it has to awkwardly cut off the shorter list in the middle of repeating it.

#Question 10: student["grades"] and student[["grades"]] look similar but return objects of different classes. Run class() on each and explain the difference in what single-bracket [ ] versus double-bracket [[ ]] return from a list.

#Answer: Single brackets [ ] give you back a smaller list with your item inside it. Double brackets [[ ]] break open the list and give you just the raw item itself.

#Question 11: Why do you think R makes a distinction between [ ] and [[ ]] for lists, but a vector only needs [ ]? Think about what a list can contain that a vector cannot.

#Answer: R does this because lists can hold many different types of data at once, so you need a way to choose between grabbing a chunk of the list or grabbing the raw data. Vectors only hold one type of data, so they only need single brackets.

# TODO: Using what you learned in Parts B and D, print only the items
# (from inventory$item) that are currently in stock (in_stock == TRUE)

```{r}
inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
```

```{r}
inventory$item[inventory$in_stock == TRUE]
```


# TODO: A new product "Ruler" priced at 15.00 and in stock (TRUE) needs
# to be added to inventory. Use append() to add "Ruler" to
# inventory$item, 15.00 to inventory$price, and TRUE to inventory$in_stock.
# (You will need three separate append() calls, one per vector.)

```{r}
inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$price <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)
```

#Question 12: In challenge-1, you combined logical indexing on one vector (in_stock) to filter a different vector (item) inside the same list. Explain, step by step, why inventory$item[inventory$in_stock] works even though item and in_stock are stored as separate elements of the list.

#Answer: Because the items and the stock status are lined up perfectly, R looks at the True/False values and only picks the items that have a "True" next to them (which are "Notebook" and "Pen").

#Question 13: Suppose a classmate stores related data as three separate, unconnected vectors (item_names, item_prices, item_stock) instead of grouping them into one list like inventory. What risks or bugs could this create as the dataset grows or gets reordered? Argue for or against using a list (or, later, a data frame) instead of separate vectors

#Answer: If you keep data in separate, unconnected lists, things can easily get mixed up (like matching a notebook with an eraser's price if you accidentally delete one item). Putting them in a single list or data frame locks them together so they never get mismatched.

#Conclusion: Vectors can only hold one type of data at a time, like all numbers or all text. Lists are flexible containers that can hold a mix of many different data types at once. Use vectors for simple math, and use lists when you need to group different kinds of information together.
